targets.descent: Joins Stanley-Burgner's P2 — descend via that route's north-face rappels, or the West Ridge if summiting.
targets.descent_text: Since this single pitch tops out at the Stanley-Burgner P1 exit, most parties continue up Stanley-Burgner or rappel back down this pitch on gear.
targets.name: Alpine Cragger's Delight

targets.descent: Scramble to the summit via the West Ridge, then use that route's rappel descent.
targets.descent_text: Since the route finishes at the top of the headwall rather than the true summit, parties scramble the remaining West Ridge terrain to the summit, then descend via the West Ridge's four-rappel descent.
targets.name: Prayer for a Friend

targets.descent: Two rappels off Solid Gold's anchors, then walk off the back side.
targets.descent_text: From the top of the route, make two rappels using the neighboring Solid Gold route's anchors, then walk off down the back (north) side.
targets.name: Sail Away

targets.descent: Descend as for Stanley-Burgner (four rappels down the north face), or make about five rappels down the right-hand couloir.
targets.descent_text: Two options: descend using the Stanley-Burgner route’s north-face rappel descent, four single-rope rappels then a 3rd-class downclimb, or make about five rappels down the couloir to the right of the route followed by easy scrambling back to the base. A single 60m rope suffices for both the ascent and the rappel descent.
targets.name: Taylor-Wood Route

targets.approach: No trail reaches Rimrock Ridge. The way in is the north end of the Ptarmigan Traverse. Start at the Cascade Pass trailhead at the end of the Cascade River Road and climb the Cascade Pass trail, then follow the traverse's climbers' path over Cache Col and down to Kool-Aid Lake, the usual first camp. The next day crosses the exposed Red Ledge below Arts Knoll and the crevassed Middle Cascade Glacier (rope up) to the Spider–Formidable col, then drops to Yang Yang Lakes, the usual second camp. On the third day the traverse climbs back to the Le Conte ridge and up the Le Conte Glacier to the col between Le Conte and Sentinel at its head. The parties on record left the traverse here, passed north of Sentinel Peak and followed the ridge east along its crest; the ridge is the divide between Flat Creek and the West Fork of Agnes Creek. Beyond the traverse the line is cross-country alpine ground with no path, and no detailed description of it is published. The Agnes Creek trail (PCT) from High Bridge runs up a different valley and does not lead to the ridge.
targets.descent_text: Retrace the ridge crest, downclimbing the rock steps and bypassing towers on the same side used on ascent.
targets.name: Standard Scramble
targets.trailhead: Cascade Pass trailhead (end of Cascade River Road)

wa_beckey_davis.approach: Standard access is via Aasgard Pass into the Core Enchantments: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek and switchbacking up to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft). From the south-end boulder field, climb Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt — the crux of the approach, hazardous under lingering snow into early July with a hidden creek/moat beneath the talus, and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Tranquil and Isolation lakes toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face, roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way. Note that this trailhead/pass can close seasonally (e.g., wildfire closures have forced parties onto the Snow Lakes Trail instead, which one trip report clocked at about 10 miles and 6,000+ ft, roughly 5 hours 44 minutes car-to-base — notably longer and with a different, less direct final approach past Lake Viviane to a climbers' trail on Prusik's south ridge).
wa_beckey_davis.descent_text: From the summit, descend the north face on four single-rope rappels using a single 60m rope, then downclimb 3rd-class ground to the climbers’ path; two optional rappels from stations climber’s right of the gully can replace that downclimb. The first rap station is an old bolt at the true summit (reported to predate the 1980s); the second rappel is built around a wedged block that looks sketchy but has held for decades of parties. Remaining stations are slung natural anchors (webbing/tat) — carry extra material to back up aged slings. From the climbers’ path, scramble around to the base of the West Ridge; some parties report one more short rappel from that notch to regain the south-face base. Total time from summit back to packs is roughly 2 hours in a typical trip report.
wa_beckey_davis.name: Beckey-Davis

wa_boving_christensen.approach: Reached via the same Core Enchantments approach as the other south-face lines: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft), then the south-end boulder field and Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep, loose scree — the approach's crux, hazardous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face, roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country navigation over slabs and talus for the final stretch.
wa_boving_christensen.descent_text: Same north-side descent as the neighboring Solid Gold and Energizer Bunny lines: locate the shared rap anchors on the north side of the ridge and make one full-length rappel (a 60m rope is standard) down to easier ground, then scramble/downclimb roughly 30 minutes back around to the base of the south face. Anchors here are natural (slung blocks/chockstones, webbing/tat) rather than bolted, and per recent forum reports have been periodically rebuilt as old tat accumulates — back up any worn-looking station.
wa_boving_christensen.name: Boving-Christensen

wa_energizer_bunny.approach: Reached via the standard Core Enchantments approach shared by the other south-face lines: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft), then the south-end boulder field and Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep loose scree — the approach's crux, hazardous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face — roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country navigation for the final approach.
wa_energizer_bunny.descent_text: Same north-side descent as neighboring Solid Gold and Boving-Christensen: find the shared rap anchors on the north side of the ridge and make one full-length rappel (a 60m rope is standard) to easier ground, then scramble/downclimb roughly 30 minutes back around to the base. Anchors are natural (slung blocks/chockstones, webbing/tat), not bolted, and have reportedly been rebuilt/relocated periodically as old tat accumulates in this area — inspect and back up any worn station.
wa_energizer_bunny.name: Energizer Bunny

wa_preacher_mountain_scramble.approach: Start at the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Trailhead (large lot at the end of FR 56). From the parking area, follow the Middle Fork Trail a short distance and cross the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River on the footbridge, then pick up the Pratt River/Pratt Connector Trail heading west/southwest — an easy, well-graded stretch of roughly 0.6 mile. Watch for the unsigned, unofficial Rainy Creek climbers' path branching off near the Rainy Creek crossing (easy to miss; GPS or a downloaded track helps here since it is not an official maintained trail). This boot path climbs steadily and steeply alongside Rainy Creek, crossing a couple of side streams/seasonal drainages around 3,100 ft — cross here rather than following the valley bottom, then angle south into steadily steepening forest to about 3,600 ft. Around 3,700 ft a short rock band forces a ~100 ft scramble move before you can side-hill in to Rainy Lake (3,800 ft), roughly 3.5-3.75 miles and 2-2.5 hours from the trailhead. The path is boot-trodden, muddy, and brushy in spots (salmonberry/blueberry brush and occasional blowdown), and largely disappears under snow through late spring — expect route-finding by feel/GPS above the lake. Rainy Lake
wa_preacher_mountain_scramble.descent_text: This is a walk-off/scramble-down, not a rappelling route — no fixed anchors or rope work are used on the standard line. Reverse the ascent line exactly: off the summit, follow the ridge north back to the 5,800 ft saddle, then descend north-northwest off the ridge to the small tarn/bench at 5,200 ft, staying well back from any cornice edge if there is snow. From the tarn, drop back down the open slopes and skirt the cliff bands on the lake (west) side of the ridge as before, downclimbing the short rock band around 3,700 ft with care (the single spot on this route with real exposure), then pick up the Rainy Creek climbers' path back down through the brush to the Pratt Connector Trail and out to the Middle Fork Trailhead. Descent time is roughly 3.5-4 hours (about 1.5 hours from summit to Rainy Lake, 2+ hours from the lake back to the car), reflecting the loose talus, brush, and route-finding on the way down being as slow as the way up. Descent-specific hazards: the mossy slab and rock band near 3,700 ft are more consequential to downclimb than to ascend and are the likeliest spot for a slip; the boot path is easy to lose in failing light or fog since it's unofficial and unmarked; and
wa_preacher_mountain_scramble.name: Standard Scramble

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.approach: Long approach into the Core Enchantments via Aasgard Pass: from the Stuart Lake Trailhead, follow the Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A junction, cross Mountaineer Creek, and switchback up to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft gain). From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining roughly 2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt, the approach's physical crux, hazardous under lingering snow (a hidden creek/moat under the talus) into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season. From the 7,841-ft pass, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn, where parties commonly bivy roughly 20 minutes from the base of Prusik's south face (there is no maintained trail for this last stretch — it's cross-country over slabs and talus). Total is roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,500+ ft one-way. Overnight camping in the Core Zone requires an Enchantments permit; the Snow Lakes Trail is a longer (9+ mile) alternative when the Stuart/Colchuck trailhead or Aasgard Pass is closed.
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.descent_text: From the summit, rappel the north side on four single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, then downclimb 3rd-class ground; one or two optional rappels right of the gully replace the downclimb. Anchors mix a bolted station near the top of pitch 1 with gear/piton anchors and slung natural features lower down — carry extra webbing to back up older tat. After the fifth rappel, scramble down to the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge and make one additional single rappel to reach easier ground before walking back to the south-face base.
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.name: Der Sportsman

wa_prusik_peak_prayer_for_a_friend.descent_text: Since the route finishes at the top of the headwall rather than the true summit, parties scramble the remaining West Ridge terrain to the summit, then descend via the West Ridge's four-rappel descent.
wa_prusik_peak_prayer_for_a_friend.name: Prayer for a Friend

wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) at the end of FS Road 7601, follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) junction. Turn left, cross Mountaineer Creek (a rock-hop/log crossing and the last reliable, easy water source for a while), and switchback up 1.6 miles through forest to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) — roughly 4.1 miles and 2,000 ft from the car. Boulder-hop along the lake's east shore to the boulder field at its south end (about 5.5 miles in, 2,500 ft gained), then pick up the climbers' trail/talus leading to the base of Aasgard Pass. Aasgard Pass itself gains about 2,000 ft in only 1.25 miles of steep, loose dirt and scree — physically the crux of the approach. It's cairned when snow-free, but in early season (often into July) snow can bridge a hidden creek/moat on the left side of the gully that has caused serious injuries and at least one fatality when climbers post-holed or glissaded into it; the slope is also avalanche-prone with a spring/early-summer snowpack. From the top of the pass (7,841 ft) descend gently into the upper Core basin past Isolation/Tranquil Lake, then continue cross-country roughly 1–1.5 miles north over
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.descent_text: From the top of Solid Gold, most parties continue to easy ground and locate the shared 'Solid Gold' rap anchors (also used to descend Sail Away and other nearby lines) on the north side of the ridge. The standard descent is a single, full-length rappel — a 60m rope is typical — down the north face, landing on easier ground below; from there it's about a 30-minute scramble/downclimb east back around to the notch below the West Ridge and the base of the south face. Some parties instead break this into two shorter rappels from the same general anchor area depending on rope length and party size/gear drag. Anchors are natural (slung blocks/chockstones with webbing/tat), not bolted, and the anchors in this immediate area (shared with the West Ridge descent) have been periodically rebuilt and relocated as old tat accumulates — inspect and back up any station that looks worn.
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.name: Solid Gold

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.approach: Long approach into the Core Enchantments via Aasgard Pass: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek and switchbacking to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft). From the south-end boulder field, ascend Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles, roughly 2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt, the approach's crux, hazardous under lingering snow into early July (hidden creek/moat beneath the talus) and avalanche-prone in shoulder season. From the pass (7,841 ft), travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, then contour below Prusik to the base of the south face and the start of the route — about 7.5–8 miles and 4,600 ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country travel over slabs and talus for the final stretch. Overnight camping in the Core requires an Enchantments permit; a longer Snow Lakes Trail alternative exists when Aasgard Pass or the Stuart/Colchuck trailhead is closed.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.descent_text: Walk east from the summit and begin the north-face rappel line on slung belay stations — natural anchors (blocks/chockstones with webbing/tat); there's little to no fixed gear at the top. Plan on four single-rope rappels of about 25-30 m, then a 3rd-class downclimb; one or two optional rappels right of the gully replace the downclimb. Figure roughly an hour from the summit back to the base if the rap line isn't backed up with other parties, which does happen since several south-face routes share this descent. Bring extra tat to back up aged webbing on the natural anchors.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.name: South Face (Burgner-Stanley)

wa_prusik_peak_taylor_wood_route.descent_text: Two options: descend using the Stanley-Burgner route’s north-face rappel descent, four single-rope rappels then a 3rd-class downclimb, or make about five rappels down the couloir to the right of the route followed by easy scrambling back to the base. A single 60m rope suffices for both the ascent and the rappel descent.
wa_prusik_peak_taylor_wood_route.name: Taylor-Wood Route

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Trail #1599) at the end of Eightmile Road/FS-7601, elev. ~3,400-3,600 ft. Hike the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed junction with the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599 continues to Stuart Lake; branch left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail). This spur crosses Mountaineer Creek on a footbridge/logs (last reliable, easy water before the basin) and then climbs a rocky, switchbacking 1.6 miles through forest and boulder fields to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft (roughly 4.1 miles and ~2,200 ft from the trailhead) - a good rest, filter-water, and gear-sort stop. Skirt the east/south shore of Colchuck Lake on climbers' trail to the large boulder field at its south end, then begin the Aasgard Pass climb: follow the outlet stream/drainage, staying climber's-left of the first band of cliffs, up steep heather, rock steps, and (in early season) snow. This is the approach crux - roughly 2,000-2,200 ft of gain in under a mile on what regulars describe as a 'jenga pile' of loose scree and talus with real fall-and-rockfall consequence; an ice axe (and crampons in early season/on residual snow) is worth carrying into July. Top out around 7,800 ft at the rim of the
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, the standard descent drops down the north side of Prusik Peak via a sequence of rappels, then traverses back to Prusik Pass to rejoin the approach line. Most parties make four rappels, then downclimb loose 3rd-class ground; one or two optional extra rappels can replace that downclimb - the first anchor is typically right at your feet on a flat spot at/near the true summit, with subsequent stations found by rappelling roughly 20-30m and looking climber's-left; anchors are fixed gear (slings/webbing 'tat' and rap rings/chains left by parties over the years, not bolted), so back them up or inspect carefully. Rappel lengths run mostly in the 25-30m range with one shorter first pitch; a single 60m rope is adequate for every station for a party of two, though a doubled 60m (30m per strand) can feel tight on the last traverse-y rappel, and parties of three often prefer a 70m rope for margin. After the last rappel, traverse west (skiers'-left) across talus back to Prusik Pass at the base of the West Ridge - this is not a walk-off from the summit itself, but the technical descent is short (well under an hour for an efficient party) and feeds directly back into the approach
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.approach: Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT trailhead) at Snoqualmie Pass West, reached via I-90 Exit 52 — this is the road-access endpoint; from the trailhead the hike itself begins on the newer rerouted Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Follow the PCT for roughly 2–2.5 miles of well-graded, well-maintained trail through old-growth forest with blueberry and salmonberry understory. At the signed junction, leave the PCT and turn left onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, following it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek in the basin, which is the one reliable natural water source on the approach (treat before drinking) — carry enough water above this point since the final scramble slopes are dry. As the trail levels out near a small tarn/pond below Red Mountain's west slope, watch for a cairn planted in the middle of the path — this marks the scramble takeoff point where you leave the maintained trail. An alternate, rougher approach follows the older, partly overgrown Commonwealth Basin Trail starting about 20 yards up from the parking lot, switchbacking directly up into the basin and rejoining near the same trail split (
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.descent_text: No rope or rappelling is used on the standard route — this is a pure walk/scramble descent. Most parties reverse the ascent line down the west-slope boot path back to the cairn and Commonwealth Creek Trail, then retrace the Commonwealth Creek Trail and PCT back to the trailhead. Some parties instead descend via the southwest ridge crest before dropping back into the boot-path drainage, which can offer more solid footing than the loose central scree the boot path sometimes follows — either line rejoins the same trail system before the pond. The overriding descent hazard is loose, fractured rock underfoot (a helmet is strongly recommended for the whole party, not just the leader, since Red Mountain's red rock is notoriously fractured and easy to kick loose onto climbers below); keep the group tight and avoid spreading out on the open scree. Do not attempt to traverse east/south off the summit toward the PCT near the Kendall Catwalk as a shortcut — that terrain quickly becomes Class 3/4 and cliffs out without a rope. Once back on the boot path, staying close to the ridge crest on the way down (rather than cutting straight down the gut of the scree slope) both preserves the trail and r
wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.name: Standard Scramble

wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail through the beaver meadows; at the first switchback past the meadows, beyond the Colchuck/Stuart Lake trail fork, leave the trail to the south on an obscure, unmaintained climbers' path, crossing Stuart Lake creek on logs, to reach the base of the northeast-facing couloir below Sherpa Peak. The path is unmaintained and can be hard to follow.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.descent_text: Most parties reverse the couloir (downclimbing or rappelling the snow/ice) back to the approach path. An alternative used by some parties is to traverse to Sherpa Pass and downclimb from there to regain camp, avoiding a full re-descent of the steepest snow.
wa_sherpa_balanced_rock_ne_couloir.name: Northeast Couloir

wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.approach: Access is the same Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead used for the West Ridge: follow the Longs Pass Trail (#1229) over Longs Pass (~6,200 ft) and down to Ingalls Creek Trail, crossing Ingalls Creek and continuing on the climbers' boot path up into the Sherpa-Argonaut basin (see West Ridge approach for that shared section). From the basin, rather than aiming for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's-left (east), traversing a grassy slope and ascending a talus/scree gully to reach the prominent notch at roughly 8,000 ft, about 600 vertical feet below and east of the true summit. Gain the ridge crest about 100 ft above (east of) the notch via class 2 terrain. This line is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge approach, and picking the correct gully/notch is the main route-finding crux; a 50m rope is worth carrying from here since the route above uses fixed rappel slings at several obstacles.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.descent_text: Most parties do not reverse the East Ridge; the accepted descent is to finish near the summit, traverse to the top of the West Ridge, and go down using the West Ridge's established rappel line (two single-rope rappels past the crux, a short scramble, another single, then a double-rope rappel to the west notch - see the West Ridge descent for full detail) before dropping back to the basin and Ingalls Creek. Some parties do reverse the East Ridge directly, especially when combining the climb with the nearby Balanced Rock feature: this involves downclimbing/rappelling a vertical chimney using chained-together fixed rappel slings, then a rappel down a steep gully to an exposed slab, then another rappel after crossing the slab, finishing with class 3 downclimbing to the 8,000-ft notch. Expect roughly 2-4 short single-rope rappels off existing (sometimes weathered) fixed slings and chains rather than full ropelength raps; a 50m rope was reported as sufficient. Back up any suspect fixed anchors with your own gear. From the notch/basin, reverse the approach: descend to Ingalls Creek Trail, cross the creek, and climb back over Longs Pass to the trailhead.
wa_sherpa_peak_east_ridge.name: East Ridge

wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.approach: The North Ridge is most commonly approached from the north via the Stuart Lake Trailhead (reached by Icicle Creek Road/Eightmile Creek Road out of Leavenworth). Follow the Stuart Lake Trail (#1599) along Mountaineer Creek roughly 3.5-4 miles, climbing gently through forest. Before reaching Stuart/Colchuck Lake, leave the maintained trail, cross Mountaineer Creek, and pick up a boot path/cairned route that climbs talus benches on the slope west of the creek, staying a couple hundred feet above the trees before dropping back toward the creek, aiming for the Argonaut-Sherpa basin. Around 5,800 ft, the route steepens into sustained loose talus leading up to the base of the North Ridge proper (~7,000 ft), a roughly 1,500-ft-tall rock feature capped by the 8,630-ft summit. At the base, contour and work climber's-right to a lower notch, where easy slabs can be scrambled before roping up. (A southern approach via Longs Pass and Ingalls Creek to Mountaineer Creek is also possible but is a longer, less direct line to this specific route.) Water is available at Mountaineer Creek but is limited higher on the talus approach - carry enough for the day. The talus benches and loose approach gully
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.descent_text: Descent is not a reversal of the North Ridge and is considered the trickiest part of the route. From the summit, downclimb/scramble a short distance to an established rappel station just west of the true summit - the top anchor of the standard West Ridge route - and make a short rappel (roughly 25-30 ft/one short pitch) down into a gully southwest of the summit. A second, shorter rappel (about 20 ft, off a slung boulder) follows; this one is optional and can be downclimbed at low 5th class by confident parties. Some parties describe this stage as two ~25m rappels rather than two short single-pitch raps, so treat the exact length as variable and carry a 50-60m rope to cover either version. Below the rappels, the terrain eases from sustained class 3 (roughly the first 500 ft) to class 2; continue southeast across loose rocky ribs and gullies, staying low to avoid cliff bands, toward the Sherpa-Argonaut saddle. The final ~1,000 ft down to treeline from the saddle is the descent's crux - loose rock only barely held in place by dirt and sand - so move carefully and stay alert for parties below. From the basin, either retrace the approach out via Mountaineer Creek and the Stuart Lake Tra
wa_sherpa_peak_north_ridge.name: North Ridge

wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.approach: From the Esmeralda Basin/Longs Pass Trailhead (end of Teanaway River Road/FS-9737, ~4,300 ft), take the Longs Pass Trail (#1229) roughly 2.3 miles and about 2,300 ft of gain to Longs Pass (~6,200 ft), a broad open saddle. From the pass, drop steeply down the north side (a boot path, with snow fingers usable for glissading in early season) about 1,300-1,400 ft to the Ingalls Creek drainage (~4,800 ft). Ford or rock-hop Ingalls Creek (can run high with early-season snowmelt) and pick up the Ingalls Creek Trail, following it right (east) about a half to full mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction. Leave the maintained trail here for a boot/climbers' path (sometimes called the "tapeworm trail") that switchbacks up through timber and brush before opening into meadow beneath Sherpa and Argonaut Peaks. Gain the rounded rib dividing the Cascadian Couloir drainage from the basin under Sherpa, then contour around 5,800 ft into the snow-holding basin below the West Ridge; kick steps up final snow/talus slopes to a common bivy/base-camp shelf around 7,400 ft (a flat table-rock area) or continue straight to the ridge base. Total gain from the car to the base of technical climbing runs roug
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.descent_text: The standard descent reverses the West Ridge using a sequence of rappels rather than downclimbing the whole route. From the summit area, two single-rope rappels lead down past the crux (5.4-5.6) pitch to a short 3rd-class scramble; this is followed by another single-rope rappel and then a longer double-rope rappel (two ropes joined, or a single 60m doubled) that returns you to the west notch below the technical climbing. Anchors are a mix of fixed slings around horns and flakes; most are solid (slings around big, well-set flakes/horns), but at least one reported station was backed by a sketchy bundle of slings wrapped around a few small loose rocks next to the actual load-bearing horn - inspect and back up questionable tat with your own gear. Some parties skip the last downclimb and instead rappel directly down the loose, dirty gully from the notch. Bring a 60m rope (or two ropes for the double-rope stretch) and extra slings/cord to replace weathered anchors. From the notch, descend scree/talus and boot path back into the basin (glissading is possible on lingering snow) to camp, then reverse the approach over Longs Pass to the trailhead. Total rappel count is commonly described as
wa_sherpa_peak_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_south_face_7.approach: From the PCT trailhead at Exit 52, hike the Pacific Crest Trail north to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction, then follow it roughly 2 miles until Red Mountain comes into view. Traverse on heather across the base of the mountain until you reach the bright red rock gully/ramp that marks the start of the route.
wa_south_face_7.descent_text: Standard descent follows the class 2 scrambling line on the west side of the south ridge back down. If the party continued up the steep summit block direct, a rappel using tree anchors with webbing and rap rings is an option.
wa_south_face_7.name: South Face
